canberra.title: Thoroughbred Park precinct to require public or community housing
canberra.snippet: At least 5 per cent of future residential development within the Thoroughbred Park Precinct in Lyneham will need to be reserved for publi...
canberra.content:
An artist’s impression of the Thoroughbred Park master plan, which could deliver up to 3200 new homes. Image: Canberra Racing Club.

At least 5 per cent of future residential development within the Thoroughbred Park Precinct in Lyneham will need to be reserved for public or income-based community housing under an update to proposed planning changes.

The move will pilot inclusionary zoning within the Territory.

The ACT Government has announced its response to consultation feedback on Draft Plan Amendment 08 – Thoroughbred Park Precinct (DPA-08), which will pave the way for a major redevelopment of racecourse land.

It said the Territory Planning Authority received 151 submissions, with around 90 per cent of respondents expressing support or in-principle support for the proposed changes.

The DPA-08 update will also require broader residential and commercial development.

Overall housing delivery numbers and staging must be determined through a developer agreement with the ACT Government to be struck once further subdivision design work has been undertaken and before residential development can be approved on the site.

Subject to further subdivision design and planning, the Thoroughbred Park site could deliver up to 3200 new homes, as well as commercial uses and a local centre.

Planning and Sustainable Development Minister Chris Steel said the government’s priority was enabling housing supply in well-located areas to secure the city’s long-term sustainable growth.

“It’s why the government is taking a transit-oriented development approach to support more housing in the places it makes most sense, near existing infrastructure and high-frequency bus and light rail stops,” he said.

Mr Steel said the government believed every new suburb in Canberra should have public housing.

He said targets already applied to residential development in new suburbs and through the release of government land.

“It’s the government’s expectation that significant, precinct-scale developments on leased land, which benefit from zoning changes, should also deliver their fair share of public community and affordable housing,” Mr Steel said.

Canberra Racing Club Chief Executive Darren Pearce said Canberra needed more well-located homes. Photo: Supplied.

The Canberra Racing Club welcomed the announcement, saying the Draft Plan Amendment would allow more Canberrans to live close to light rail in the city’s inner north while retaining Thoroughbred Park’s thriving racing, training and events centre.

The club’s masterplan would retain around 60 per cent of the precinct for racing, training and events, and develop the remaining 40 per cent.

Canberra Racing Club Chief Executive Darren Pearce said Canberra needed more well-located homes and Thoroughbred Park would make a significant contribution.

“This is perhaps the best opportunity in the Territory to create a thriving community for its future,” he said.

“This precinct gives people the chance to live a short light rail ride from the city, and we can do that while maintaining our thriving racing, training and events centre for the community to enjoy.”

Mr Pearce said the rigorous community consultation process attracted strong support and the club looked forward to getting to work on the masterplan.

Thoroughbred Park currently hosted 150 events each year, including 25 race days, major food and cultural festivals, Digifest, Canberra Cars N Coffee, private, corporate and community events such as the annual Children’s Christmas Party.

Independent analysis by IER found that thoroughbred racing contributed more than $80 million a year to the ACT economy and supported more than 500 local jobs.

Mr Pearce said that the club, as a not-for-profit, invested back into the venue, sport and the broader community.

“Income from development will help us maintain the facilities that our racing and events communities rely on and grow how the club backs local organisations through initiatives like the Canberra Community Chest,” he said.

“We understand the community’s need for quality services, for social and community housing and for inclusive neighbourhoods where people want to live.”

Mr Pearce urged MLAs to support the amendment.

The amendment also updates the indicative zoning of the pony club site (Block 1 Section 70 Lyneham) to Community Facility Zone to retain the site for future long-term community or educational use.

The government said this did not impact the Canberra Riding Club Pony Club’s current lease for the site, which was agreed for 10 years in 2025.

Kamberra Winery and the veterinary site have been removed from DPA-08 after feedback from the National Capital Authority.

Potential zoning changes for these sites will be considered as part of future planning work for the broader Northern Gateway and progressed through an updated Draft Plan Amendment 09 (DPA-09). It is expected to be brought forward early next year.

The revised DPA-08 has been referred to the Legislative Assembly Standing Committee on Environment and Planning, which may conduct an inquiry.

The Consultation Report and revised draft amendment are available on ACT Planning.

canberra.title: Light rail to Woden given environmental tick of approval from Commonwealth
canberra.snippet: Light rail Stage 2B from Commonwealth Park to Woden has been given Australian Government environmental approval, with conditions. The app...
canberra.content:
27 November 2026

Start the conversation

Light rail Stage 2B will dramatically change the Commonwealth Avenue landscape. Photo: ACT Government.

Light rail Stage 2B from Commonwealth Park to Woden has been given Australian Government environmental approval, with conditions.

The approval is valid for 10 years and moves the project a step closer to delivering a north-south mass-transit spine, enabling commuters to travel directly between Gungahlin and Woden.

The ACT Government said the environmental approval was a significant milestone for light rail Stage 2B, but the project must still complete the Territory’s environmental assessment process, which is expected to conclude by the end of 2026.

The conditions cover managing impacts to nationally significant environmental values, including multiple heritage places, objects and values, and to threatened species such as the Gang-gang Cockatoo, Superb Parrot and Golden Sun Moth.

They also include the requirement for a tree planting management plan which must confirm the number of trees to be cleared during construction. New plantings must amount to at least double the number lost.

The proposed removal of trees along Commonwealth Avenue has been particularly contentious.

The loss of the 100-year-old Charles Weston plantings of Himalayan cedars from the central median from Albert Hall to Coronation Drive and large-scale tree loss from the verges on both sides from the front of Hotel Canberra to the Albert Street intersection was slammed in a submission from the Inner South Canberra Community Council, which called the EIS defective.

The current 100-year-old cedars will be replaced by new plantings of pin oaks.

The council’s submission also questioned the choice of the State Circle East alignment around Parliament House.

It quoted the GML Heritage Report, which said: “The impacts on the heritage places associated with the State Circle East alignment will extensively alter the historic character and geometry of Canberra’s highly significant planned landscape, changing the expression of the designed city plan prepared by the Griffins and implemented by subsequent custodians, which forms the underlying structure for the entire expression of the unique and iconic urban design of Canberra.”

Environmental approval allows light rail Stage 2B to advance to further planning and detailed design stages.

Planning and Sustainable Development Minister Chris Steel said light rail was central to delivering a mass-transit system to support Canberra’s sustainable growth, connecting urban villages and new housing along the line.

“The transport infrastructure proposed as part of the project will ensure that more Canberrans can access high-quality frequent public transport on the southside,” he said.

“Light Rail Stage 2B will also connect residents with the city’s major employment hub in Barton and Parkes, which continues to grow with the construction of the National Security Office Precinct.”

The Environmental Impact Statement (EIS) was lodged with the Australian and ACT Governments in June 2026, following a detailed consultation process which considered more than 230 submissions from community and stakeholders.

It was assessed under the Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Act (EPBC Act).

The ACT Government is also progressing the Southern Gateway Framework, which will play an important role in shaping long-term land use in the corridor between the City and Woden.

Light Rail Stage 2A from the city to Commonwealth Park is expected to be complete next year, ahead of passenger services commencing in early 2028.

canberra.title: Elderly cyclist, young man allegedly assaulted and robbed in Queanbeyan
canberra.snippet: A man has been arrested and charged with six offences over the alleged assault and robbery of two people in Queanbeyan. An 85-year-old ma...
canberra.content:
27 November 2026

Start the conversation

A 21-year-old man was charged with six offences over the alleged assaults and robberies in Queanbeyan. Photo: Michelle Kroll.

A man has been arrested and charged with six offences over the alleged assault and robbery of two people in Queanbeyan.

An 85-year-old man was riding his bicycle on Trinculo Place at about 7 am on Wednesday (25 November) when he was approached by a stranger and allegedly assaulted.

The elderly man rode away, but was allegedly followed by the man to the Monaro Street Bridge. It’s alleged the cyclist was again assaulted and had his wallet stolen.

Police officers were called to Monaro Street but the unknown man had already left the scene.

Officers were then called at about 7:10 am to nearby Mowatt Street, Queanbeyan, where a 23-year-old man was also allegedly assaulted and threatened.

The 85-year-old man and 23-year-old man were treated by NSW Ambulance paramedics before being taken to hospital for further treatment.

When police arrived to Mowatt Street, they arrested a 21-year-old man.

It’s alleged the man resisted police, with one officer punched in the face.

After using OC spray to apprehend the man, he was taken to Queanbeyan Police Station.

There he was charged with demand property by force with intent to steal, aggravated robbery, assault occasioning actual bodily harm, stalk/intimidate intend fear physical etc harm (personal), assault police officer in execution of duty without actual bodily harm, and hinder or resist police officer int the execution of duty.

The man appeared in Queanbeyan Local Court on Thursday 26 November, where he was formally refused bail.

The 21-year-old is scheduled to reappear on Tuesday 8 December.

Police are still searching for a black backpack and a wallet. Anyone with information about the whereabouts of these items has been asked to contact Queanbeyan Police or Crime Stoppers on 1800 333 000.

Original Article published by Claire Fenwicke on About Regional.

canberra.title: ‘Blood’ on Woolies knee-high security gates raise questions about their hygiene
canberra.snippet: Questions about the hygiene of Woolworths’ new knee-high security gates have once again sparked debate about their practicality. On...
canberra.content:
The hygiene of Woolworths’ security gates has been questioned after one customer took photos of what he believed was blood on the pylons. Photo: Gary Sharman.

Questions about the hygiene of Woolworths’ new knee-high security gates have once again sparked debate about their practicality.

On Wednesday (25 November), Gary Sharman, a regular shopper at Woolworths Tuggeranong, took a picture of the horizontal bars at the store entrance with what he believed was blood smeared across them.

Mr Sharman said he initially noticed the ‘blood’ on the gates the day before, but assumed it would be cleaned up. A day later, he said the stain was still on the gates.

Fed up, Mr Sharman took a picture of the gates before asking staff to clean them up. He said the staff replied that they would look into it.

“I saw the blood and genuinely said, ‘Yuck!’ out loud,” he said.

“I triped to tiptoe around it because it was so gross, not to mention unhygienic. I thought maybe it was a one-off, but I came back the next day, and it was still there.

“I thought, nope, that’s too far; I have to do something about this. I brought it up with one of the staff who was at the checkouts, and they told me it was a very common complaint.”

The new type of security gates, made up of 8-10 horizontal, pushable pylons, have been on trial at Woolworths’ South Point and Belconnen stores since June.

Woolworths said at the time the new gates were being used to deter would-be thieves from leaving via the front of the store.

“These gates are one of a number of initiatives to minimise retail crime across our store network, acting as part of a broader program to enhance safety for our team members and customers while helping to prevent theft,” a Woolworths spokesperson said at the time.

Woolworths introduced the new gates back in June. Photo: Jarryd Rowley.

Now five months into the trial, Mr Sharman said he believes it has missed the mark and, by trying to stop thieves from leaving, has created a worse customer experience.

“In an ideal world, I wish they would just go back to the automatic gates,” he said.

“I understand that Woolworths wants to look after their stock, but it made more sense to have the automatic one.

“You didn’t have to physically push or touch them, it wouldn’t open from inside the store, and you could still push prams and trolleys through them with no issue.

“The current gates just aren’t practical. If thieves want to get through the gates, they’ll find a way. The only people getting punished are the customers.”

Mr Sharman said he has made a complaint to the ACT Health Protection Service, stating the gates pose a public health risk.

“It’s definitely a massive step back. I haven’t spoken to a single person who thinks they’re a good idea,” he said.

“I’ve spoken to people who have had kids smacked in the face, causing them to have blood noses. Others, who have wheelchairs, said they can’t get in.

“On top of the hygiene issue, where the pylons are constantly rubbing on people’s skin, it appears to also be a safety issue.”

A spokesperson for Woolworths said: “[Woolworths] takes the safety and cleanliness of our stores very seriously.

“Our stores follow regular cleaning routines across all high-touch surfaces and entry points.

“If a customer is ever unhappy with their experience, we encourage them to speak with our store team or contact our Customer Hub directly so we can look into it.”

canberra.title: Canberra grapes and Riverina winemakers are the perfect blend for an award-winning Shiraz
canberra.snippet: Few wineries can claim a heritage like McWilliam’s. Established in 1877, it’s helped to shape the Riverina’s winemaking tradi...
canberra.content:
Wine distributor Cameron Smith and Calabria Family Wines representative Tanya Todorova accept the award from chair of judges Marcus Statchel (centre). Photo: SDP Media.

Few wineries can claim a heritage like McWilliam’s. Established in 1877, it’s helped to shape the Riverina’s winemaking traditions. In addition to sourcing grapes from the Riverina region, McWilliam’s also sources parcels of fruit from regions such as Hilltops, Tumbarumba and Canberra. It’s the Canberra region collaboration that has won it a prestigious trophy at the Melbourne Royal Wine Awards.

Winemaker Stephanie Sheather has been working with McWilliam’s since 2013, starting out as a cellar hand and working her way up. She’s pleased to see the Riverina being acknowledged as the region modernises and makes more premium wines.

“This region was known for quite some time as a bulk processing region, but there’s some wonderful growers and winemakers here,” she told Region.

“I’d love for the region to be seen as not just commercial. We do that very well here, but we also do some smaller premium batches and have a wider range of varieties: sparkling wines, table wines, fortified wines and even botrytis. We make a bit of everything and do it very well.”

The trophy for Best NSW/ACT Shiraz was won by the McWilliam’s 660 Shiraz, made using grapes grown by Russell Kerrison at Quarry Hill, just outside Canberra. The vineyard was planted in 1999 on the site of the quarry which supplied materials to build the Barton Highway.

Stephanie said that, ultimately, the quality of the wine was determined by the quality of the grapes.

“The quarry would have unearthed different minerals and rocks in the hill, so the terroir and soil is different to others in the region,” Stephanie said.

“As a cool climate region, Canberra gets frosts, hailstorms – it can be quite unpredictable. But we’re lucky in that the shiraz up there is on the side of the hill that’s quite sheltered so it’s relatively protected.

“Russell really puts his heart and soul into that vineyard, and then we just try not to stuff it up!”

The 660 Shiraz was described by judges as “a vibrant cool-climate Shiraz that reflects the unique character of the Canberra district. Expressive aromas of dark berries, plum and black pepper are complemented by subtle spice and savoury undertones. The palate is medium-bodied and finely structured, with bright acidity, elegant tannins and a long, balanced finish that showcases both power and finesse”.

McWilliam’s was also awarded a Trophy for Consistency of Excellence for the Hanwood Estate 20 Year Tawny. Photo: McWilliam’s.

McWilliam’s also won an award for its 20 Year Old Tawny. The winery has historically had a strong focus on fortified wines, and was awarded the Trophy for Consistency of Excellence.

The Melbourne Royal Wine Awards was established in 1883 and is considered one of the most prestigious in the country, with entries from all over Australia. Other notable trophies at the awards include the Jimmy Watson for Best Young Red Wine, which in 2024 was won by Canberra region’s Four Winds Vineyard for its 2023 Shiraz. This year, the Jimmy Watson went to Pooley Wines in Tasmania’s Coal River Valley for its 2025 Syrah.

Stephanie is excited to see Riverina wines continue to receive awards and recognition. It’s a region with a long history, but one that makes it well suited to the trends of today.

“Griffith has quite a strong Italian heritage dating back to the settlement of the town. Italian immigrants purchased blocks of land and planted what people might call ‘alternative’ varieties. The grapes they brought across – like Fiano, Sangiovese, Vermentino – are becoming more common and popular with consumers as well as the broader wine community,” she said.

“And these grapes are stronger and are able to withstand the heat because they have thicker skin and require less water. So it’s nice to see some of these emerging varieties coming out and people playing around with the styles.”

McWilliam’s Wines is well known for the Big Wine Barrel, its large wine-barrel shaped cellar door, which was built in Hanwood in 1973. It was closed for several years but reopened in August 2023, two years after the Griffith-based Calabria family took ownership of the McWilliam’s brand.

See the full list of winners at the Melbourne Royal Wine Awards.

Find out more about McWilliam’s via their website, or check out their Facebook and Instagram.

Original Article published by Lucy Ridge on Region Riverina.

australia.title: Jess Wilson’s plan for Melbourne sewage plants risks water and wetlands without bringing debt down, experts say
australia.snippet: Academic says Victorian Liberal proposal to lease treatment plants and generate profit with no compromise of services ‘a total furphy’ Vi...
australia.content:
Experts have warned the Victorian Liberals’ plan to lease Melbourne’s sewage treatment plants is a “smoke and mirrors” way to pay off debt that risks compromising the state’s water resources and crucial wetlands for nearly a century.

On Thursday – two days out from the election – the opposition leader, Jess Wilson, announced plans for a 90-year lease of the Eastern and Western treatment plants, which process the vast majority of the city’s sewage and are run by Melbourne Water.

The lease is estimated to be worth $9.2bn, with Wilson saying there would be “no change” to water bills or the Essential Services Commission’s regulation of prices across the sector.

Experts are concerned the move could lead to worse services for Victorians, and compromise vital wetlands in Melbourne’s west.

Dr Erin O’Donnell, a water law expert at the University of Melbourne Law School, said given the prices would still be regulated, it would be difficult for private companies to extract value from the services, and the money gained from the lease would amount to only about 5% of the debt held by the state.

“I wouldn’t even classify it as a sugar hit – it’s smoke and mirrors,” O’Donnell said.

“This will not make a significant dent in the debt that Victoria holds, and we are compromising the future of our water resources 90 years into the future.”

O’Donnell said Victoria already required corporations to pay significant dividends to the state government, with strict controls over pricing. It means there is no profit to be realised for private owners while also delivering the same quality of services, she said.

“Victoria has some of the lowest water charges of anywhere in Australia and the idea that there is unrealised profit that could be safely stripped out without compromising those services is a total furphy – I can’t say it any clearer.”

O’Donnell and Prof Stuart Khan, a water quality expert and head of the school of civil engineering at the University of Sydney, both pointed to the UK privatisation of water services in the 1980s under Margaret Thatcher as an example of how it can all go wrong.

The privatisation has been described as an “unmitigated disaster”, with hopes the Burnham Labour government will renationalise the utilities following years of declining services, and rivers polluted by private operators.

Khan said the UK’s services were privatised without guardrails around pricing or minimum standards of services.

“Practically every single river in England now has sewage contamination in it,” he said. “That’s the sort of situation that we need to make sure that we avoid because obviously private players are only going to be there if there’s a profit to be made.”

Victoria’s Labor state minister for the environment, Jaclyn Symes, pointed to the UK system and said it resulted in bills going up by 40% and “left wildlife swimming in a toilet”.

Khan said the NSW government’s privatisation of Sydney desalination plant could be a model that would work.

“It’s price regulated. It has requirements around managing water quality and they put drinking water straight into Sydney’s distribution system,” he said, adding it also has requirements from NSW Health and the state’s environmental protection agency.

Biodiversity Council member and waterbird and wetland expert Prof Richard Kingsford warned the privatisation could have disastrous consequences for Melbourne’s environment, including the wetland in the Western treatment plant at Werribee.

In 1983, the site was listed under the Ramsar convention as an internationally significant wetland, and more than 300 species of bird – including many threatened species such as the orange bellied-parrot – have been recorded there.

“It’s absolutely one of the more important wetland systems,” Kingsford said.

“I think it’s becoming increasingly important because we’ve had more wetlands drying up, less flooding and, particularly in dry times, it provides dependable habitat.”

Kingsford said privatisation “would likely drive different ways of management that might actually not have any consideration for the environmental value of the system”.

O’Donnell said it was “extraordinarily disingenous” for the Liberal party to announce the policy less than two days before the election when many Victorians had already voted.

“I think there is a real concern there, in terms of the openness around their policies [and] this will have significant implications for things like a swimmable Birrarung [Yarra River],” she said.

A Victorian Liberal party spokesperson said the criticism was “another desperate scare campaign by Labor.”

“We are not selling Melbourne Water. It was Labor that had a plan to privatise Melbourne Water. What we are proposing is a lease. When you lease something you still own it.

“The proceeds will be used to reduce Victoria’s debt and interest bill.”

The proposal has already been thrown into doubt after One Nation’s Victorian leader, Warren Pickering, vowed to block it should the party hold the balance of power after the election.

The Greens leader, Ellen Sandell, also promised to “fight Jess Wilson’s privatisation agenda tooth and nail should her Coalition form government”.

australia.title: Jesse Baird and Luke Davies’ murders rocked Sydney’s LGBTQI+ heart. Three years on, sentencing will cast a shadow over Mardi Gras
australia.snippet: The couple’s deaths at the hands of Beau Lamarre-Condon sent a bolt through Pride celebrations. Their community says they will never be f...
australia.content:
Jesse Baird couldn’t wait for his friend’s Mardi Gras party in 2024.

Michael Brown had been planning to host the celebration and knew people were likely going to float in and out as they hopped between Pride events that weekend in Sydney.

“I thought he was going to some other party but he’s like, ‘No, I’m definitely coming to your house. I can’t wait for your Mardi Gras party,’” the makeup artist from Sydney tells Guardian Australia.

“His excitement was making me excited because he was almost like a little kid.”

Though Baird had come out later in life than some of his gay friends, at this point the 26-year-old was “so accepting of himself, really happy with himself and loving life”, Brown says.

But he would never get to go to the party.

On 19 February 2024, he and his new boyfriend, 29-year-old Luke Davies, were murdered in Baird’s Paddington home.

Their bodies would not be found for eight days, and it wasn’t until Wednesday, two-and-a-half years later, that the police officer who murdered them was found guilty.

In the aftermath, friends and family members of Baird and Davies have shared memories of their loved ones.

Brown recalls meeting Baird for the first time in mid-2023.

“Straight away, it was just that smile,” he says. “When certain people smile, it lights up their eyes as well – like the whole face – and that’s what reminds me of Jesse.”

Their friendship sprang from a conversation about the AFL legend Buddy Franklin, who was a close friend of Brown’s and a player Baird admired.

Within months, they were lunching, partying and having deep conversations.

Davies’ brother John Davies told Channel Nine: “[Luke] was the most beautiful soul there is; not one person ever had a bad thing to say about him. Every person he’d come across, he would have such an impact on their life.”

In a Substack tribute, another friend of Baird’s, Jesse D’Vauz, describes getting to know him. D’Vauz had found himself alone in a big new city after moving to Sydney, and was on the dancefloor with Baird after their mutual friends had peeled away.

“Titanium came on and Jesse yelled, ‘This is my song! Let’s dance!’” he writes.

“He took my hand and pulled it up into the air. He wasn’t trying to impress me, or perform, or turn the night into something it wasn’t. He just wanted us both to enjoy it.

“Looking back, that’s what his kindness always looked like. Not a grand gesture, just wanting the person next to him to be having as good a time as he was.”

As the 10-week trial got under way, these stories rippled out from Baird and Davies’ close circles, resonating through Australia’s LGBTQI+ communities and affecting people they had never met.

Melbourne-based postgraduate student Jon Ricketson, who attended the double murder trial every day as part of his research, says the couple’s lives have left a mark on him.

“It is this confluence of factors: these were young, gay men living in this very particular part of Sydney with everything ahead of them,” he says.

“Every queer person I know has some kind of distant connection, or interest, or strong emotional reaction, and felt its impact in a real, visceral way.”

Brown was preparing to go to Gaytimes festival in Victoria when he heard news of the men’s disappearance.

“It happened at this particular moment in the summer when queer festivities were gearing up – moments of incredible connectedness and fun and joy – and it was such a bolt through the middle of those celebrations,” he says.

“Those Instagram images of Luke and Jesse at the Pink concert were indelible.

“Then the final confirmation came the following week, that was when the shock and horror gave way to something like public grief.”

On the Friday before the Mardi Gras parade, hundreds of mourners gathered, laid flowers and signed condolence books at a public vigil held for the two men.

“It wasn’t just friends, so many people in the crowd said, ‘We didn’t know them at all,’” Brown remembers.

“There were a lot of silences, you could hear little whispers and little chants and people saying they’ve come from ages away just to be there, to feel like they were part of something – saying goodbye, saying, ‘We love you and you’re never going to be forgotten.’”

When it was revealed Beau Lamarre-Condon, a serving police officer who had casually dated Baird, had been charged with their murders, historic tensions between the LGBTQ+ community and police were brought to the fore.

Police were initially asked not to march in that year’s Mardi Gras parade before a compromise was reached, allowing officers to participate out of uniform.

“The case crosses into so many parts of queer life,” Ricketson says.

“The queer community across the world but in New South Wales [especially] has had a complicated, fraught and violent history with the police … I’m sure many queer people would relate to that feeling of discomfort when you’re in the presence of police.”

For Brown, the police presence at the parade was far from front of mind.

He had spent days reading the news, “ugly crying” in his home and churning through all the things he wished he had done differently.

Brown was going to cancel his party. He didn’t feel like having people over.

But his friends said: “No, no, no. Jesse thought it was happening, we’re doing it, we’re doing a tribute.”

The night of the party, they put up a photo of Baird, lit candles around it and, as a community, vowed to celebrate and remember the two men.

“We just wanted to make sure he was in the room with us because he really wanted to come,” Brown says.

When he heard the men’s murderer had been found guilty on Wednesday, Brown felt relief wash over him, knowing there would be justice for the families.

Lamarre-Condon’s sentencing will be on 11 March 2027, once again tainting the time when Baird and Davies’ friends would normally be celebrating Pride.

When that day comes, Brown will only be thinking of the last time he saw the couple.

The night before they died, Baird and Davies had just returned from a weekend away in the Hunter Valley and were meeting their friends at the Beresford, which is a gathering place for the LGBTQ+ community.

“They just looked so happy walking in together – it was beautiful,” he says. “I’ve got both their faces in my mind.”

australia.title: Labor faces prospect of electoral wipeout in Victoria as voters turn to Liberals and One Nation
australia.snippet: Former ALP strategist says Ben Carroll government at risk of losing more than 30 seats in Saturday’s election, to fall behind Pauline Han...
australia.content:
The Victorian Labor government is facing an electoral wipeout after 12 years in office as the state heads to the polls on Saturday.

Polling during the campaign has consistently pointed to a Coalition victory. The final Newspoll, released on Thursday, showed the Coalition 15 points ahead on a two-party-preferred basis.

If replicated across the state, that swing would translate into 67 seats for the Coalition – comfortably above the 45 needed to form a majority government. The Liberals and Nationals currently hold a combined 29 seats.

But the scale of Labor’s defeat remains unclear. Some polls have suggested the party could fall behind One Nation into third place, with its primary vote only marginally ahead of the Greens.

“Right now, definitely, it’s going to be a Coalition government, but how Labor, the Greens and One Nation are going to go – that’s going to be a lot more chaotic,” said Ben Raue, an electoral analyst and founder of the Tally Room.

Raue said One Nation’s prospects will depend heavily on which party it is competing against in each seat. One Nation is targeting 12 lower house seats. It will field candidates in all lower house seats.

In contests with the Liberals or Nationals, One Nation would fare “very badly” because about 80% of preferences from other parties would flow to the Coalition partners, he said.

“The places where they are likely going to be strongest are those outer suburban seats they could take off Labor,” Raue said.

“They probably couldn’t take them if Labor was in a stronger position. Labor is so weak right now that those areas can come into play.”

On Friday, Labor campaign sources said they were bracing for a “wild night”, with three- and four-cornered contests expected across the state. Internal research suggested the party could lose up to 10 seats to One Nation, prompting former premier Steve Bracks to urge voters not to abandon Labor.

One Nation’s state leader, Warren Pickering, tempered expectations, telling reporters on Friday: “We have effectively got one state member, anything more than that is a success. We have already won.”

Kos Samaras, a former Labor strategist who is now a pollster with Redbridge, said Labor was at risk of losing more than 30 seats – a figure he described as conservative. The party currently holds 54.

“If they come out of this with 20 seats, it’s a really good result,” Samaras said. “Below that, without stating the obvious, it’s a massive problem.”

Samaras said Labor was likely to lose several regional seats, including Ripon, Bendigo East – held by former premier Jacinta Allan – Bendigo West, Eureka and Wendouree. The party could also lose seats across the Geelong region that it has held since 1999, including Bellarine, Geelong, Lara and South Barwon.

In Melbourne’s south-east, Carrum and Frankston were also at risk of switching from Labor to One Nation. Further out, Labor was not in contention in Bass, Hastings and Pakenham, where the contest was shaping as a fight between the Liberals and One Nation, he said.

In the north-west, Melton, Sunbury and Sydenham were also potential One Nation gains. Meanwhile, the Liberals are expected to pick up eastern suburbs seats including Ashwood, Bayswater, Box Hill, Glen Waverley and Ringwood.

The Liberals are even confident in the premier’s own seat of Niddrie and neighbouring Essendon.

Labor’s inner-city seats of Footscray, Northcote and Pascoe Vale were each a “coin toss” between the party and the Greens, Samaras said. But Greens sources are confident about the seats, as well as Prahran, which it lost to the Liberals at a 2025 byelection.

Samaras said the margins in many seats would be fragile.

“The Coalition is going to win 55 to 60 seats but someone only has to breathe in the wrong direction and they lose 20,” he said.

The premier, Ben Carroll, made his final pitch to voters on Friday, saying while Labor had “made some mistakes”, it was the only party on the side of workers in the middle of a cost-of-living crisis.

“We won’t fight against you. We won’t make cuts. We certainly won’t say one thing and then, after several million people have voted, then go and do another,” he said, in reference to the Coalition’s pre-budget costings on Thursday, which detailed a plan to privatise the sewage system.

The Coalition leader, Jess Wilson, called the poll a “a referendum on four more years of Labor”.

“Tomorrow Victorians have an opportunity to change the direction of the state we all love and we have the plan to get started,” she said.

If elected on Saturday, she will become Victoria’s youngest leader since federation and the first woman to be popularly elected as the state’s premier – a feat neither Allan nor Joan Kirner achieved.

  • Additional reporting by Bertin Huynh and Henry Belot

australia.title: NSW Labor is ‘trampling over party principles’ with preselections by captain’s call, members say
australia.snippet: Exclusive: Ryde councillor Penny Pedersen was asked by Labor head office not to nominate for Lane Cove in March state election Get our br...
australia.content:
Labor’s New South Wales leadership has been accused of alienating members and undermining the democratic process, after multiple state election candidates were preselected by “captain’s call” instead of the rank and file.

The premier, Chris Minns, announced on Friday that commercial litigator Jade Tyrrell will be Labor’s candidate for the marginal Liberal-held seat of Lane Cove at March’s state election.

He confirmed the nomination is the latest to be sent to Labor’s national executive, a procedure which bypasses a preselection by branch members.

Guardian Australia understands that Labor’s candidate at the 2023 election, Ryde councillor Penny Pedersen – who reduced the margin of the previously safe Liberal seat by almost two-thirds – was asked not to nominate by Labor head office, in favour of another candidate, Vivienne Moxham-Hall, a former adviser to the health minister, Ryan Park.

After Moxham-Hall – who was subsequently endorsed by local members – withdrew her nomination this month, citing a change in her current workplace policy, Tyrrell has become the second candidate to be chosen for the electorate by party leadership.

A local Labor source said Moxham-Hall and Tyrrell were both highly qualified candidates, but local rank-and-file members had been “strung along” by head office.

“We’ve been trying to win this seat since 2011 and the first time we get close they say all of a sudden, ‘No, we’re imposing a different candidate,’” they said.

In recent weeks, Minns and the party’s organisational wing in Sussex Street have faced accusations of making “captain’s calls” on candidates in multiple winnable or Labor-held seats.

This includes the premier publicly endorsing candidates in seats without rank-and-file preselections, in some cases before the national executive had signed off on them. The candidates in 12 seats for March’s election have been sent to the national executive so far.

Under Labor party rules, the 21-member executive, which includes prime minister Anthony Albanese, can intervene over rank-and-file preselections to choose candidates. While other candidates can still nominate, a recommendation by NSW party leadership in one candidate’s favour is considered a fait accompli.

In the safe Liberal seat of Epping, the premier last week endorsed former Liberal staffer and councillor Tanya Raffoul as Labor’s candidate, a move which has drawn some internal anger.

Although another Labor member Benson Koschinski nominated against Raffoul, the national executive endorsed Raffoul’s candidacy in a unanimous vote.

Guardian Australia understands every member of the executive subbed out to allow proxy voters. NSW minister Rose Jackson subbed in for Albanese, while other proxies included staffers from the premier’s and senior NSW ministers’ offices.

One senior Labor source, speaking on the condition of anonymity to discuss internal matters, said it was not unusual for proxies to be used when ballots were conducted on short notice, but others said it was highly unusual for every single member to nominate one.

Multiple senior branch sources said sending preselections to the national executive had become too regular.

One said it had become “the norm instead of the extraordinary”, while another said it was undermining Labor institutions.

“How does this help the health of the party?” they said.

‘Not running a charity’

In Terrigal, another marginal Liberal seat – and the only one held by the Coalition on the central coast – the deputy premier, Prue Car, on Thursday announced local high school principal Lisa Wicks as Labor’s candidate.

The party’s candidate in 2023, Sam Boughton, had been re-endorsed by members but recently dropped out following a family tragedy and has endorsed Wicks.

Guardian Australia understands that Wicks was first introduced to members at a branch meeting as a new member of the party on Sunday.

In a meeting with members at another local branch on Wednesday – the evening before the announcement – a senior member of Labor’s organisational wing said Wicks would be the party’s candidate after the preselection had been sent to the national executive without any other nominations.

One local member said some at the meeting accepted this, but others supported a preselection “in order for the rank and file to be given their say, after which we would probably have been satisfied with who had been chosen democratically, as is our right”.

A senior Labor party source said the unforeseen circumstances which led to candidates dropping out in Lane Cove and Terrigal had made the use of the national executive necessary.

On Tuesday, Minns said the preselection for Rockdale, a seat held by the sports minister, Steve Kamper, who is a close political ally, would be decided by the executive, following a similar announcement last week about another sitting minister Anoulack Chanthivong.

The intervention in Rockdale has drawn criticism from the former Labor upper house member Shaoquett Moselmane, who said he would have nominated for a rank and file preselection.

“Such action represents yet another example of a party leadership that is increasingly detached from the needs and aspirations of the majority of party members,” he said.

“It’s an act of trampling over party principles of fairness, transparency and honesty in preselection.”

Speaking alongside Tyrrell on Friday, Minns said he understood “concern and consternation about some of those processes”, but cited the threat posed by One Nation which is consistently polling a close second to Labor in NSW.

“I have to put the best team on the path, I have to put outstanding candidates, ones that have got deep connections with the local community, an element of the community that have traditionally voted maybe for a conservative candidate” he said.

Tyrrell, a Labor party member of 15 years, said she had grown up in Hunters Hill, which is in the Lane Cove electorate, and now lived in Waverton, which is in the neighbouring electorate of North Shore.

Guardian Australia understands Pedersen had been involved in monthly street stalls after the 2025 federal election success of local Labor member, Jerome Laxale, but that the party head office had asked for this campaigning to pause earlier this year.

In response to a series of detailed questions sent to NSW Labor head office and the premier, Guardian Australia was referred to comments Minns made at press conferences endorsing the candidates for Winston Hills and Wallsend, both preselections sent to the national executive.

Minns told reporters in Wallsend that Labor was “not running a charity” but a political party.

A Sussex Street source said if the candidates sent to the national executive were elected in March, there would be a “massive injection of talent in Macquarie Street”, including potential future ministers.

Pedersen and Moxham-Hall have been contacted for comment.

australia.title: ‘I felt a zap race through my body’: what happens when someone is hit by lightning?
australia.snippet: Tens of thousands of people experience strikes each year. What are the effects of a current five times hotter than the sun – and how can ...
australia.content:
Caitlin Thomas recalls knowing that something terrible had happened but not fully understanding what.

She and her partner had arrived at a music festival some 270km north of Melbourne in the early afternoon and began setting up their tents and a gazebo for shade when the sky suddenly turned dark and the rain became incredibly heavy. A huge gust of wind picked up and Thomas asked her partner to hold on to the gazebo so it wouldn’t fly away. “He then asked me to hold on to it also so he could crack open his beer.”

“We heard this huge crack of thunder which felt like it shook the ground underneath it,” she says. “It almost felt like we were in a dome of thunder. Within three seconds everything was in a whiteout, and I felt a zap race through my body.”

She saw her partner, Harry Gordon, lying on the ground in the foetal position, holding his left arm, not moving.

“I remember the fear of not knowing if he was okay. I recall the second my body and brain linked as I looked down at my left leg and left arm and could not feel anything … As soon as I saw Harry move, I began sprinting for my life, searching for help. I remember looking down at my body running but not being able to feel anything.”

Thomas and Gordon had been struck by lightning in a freak storm at the three-day Strawberry Fields music festival in Tocumwal, on the Victoria-New South Wales border, on 20 November.

Grant Kirkby, a lightning risk mitigation expert from Western Australia, believes they were affected by an “upward streamer leader”.

“As lightning begins to travel downwards from a thundercloud, it creates an extremely strong electrical field at ground level,” he says. “In response to this electrical field, small channels of electricity can start travelling upwards from the ground and [through] objects such as trees, buildings, metal structures and even people.

“In effect, these upward electrical currents are competing to connect with the approaching lightning. When one successfully connects, it completes the electrical pathway between the cloud and the ground, resulting in the bright lightning strike that we see.”

The gazebo’s metal frame – an excellent conductor – would have allowed the electrical current to travel through it easily, he explains. So, what Thomas and Gordon experienced would have been an electrical discharge rather than a direct strike, similar to what happened to a Chinese weather presenter on live TV who was holding an umbrella.

“A person does not necessarily have to be standing at the point where lightning strikes the ground to be injured,” Kirkby says.

Lightning (which contains a current five times hotter than the surface of the sun) can injure or kill someone indirectly by the electricity that spreads through the ground, jumps from a nearby object or travels along metal, as well as upward streamers. About 95% of people are struck indirectly, and both direct and indirect strikes can be fatal.

Thomas says her experience was “extremely painful, almost like every muscle had contracted at the same time”. It left her feeling weak and dizzy, with an instant headache.

But she and Gordon were extremely lucky. After being taken to hospital by ambulance and monitored for several hours, the 23-year-olds were given the all-clear.

Globally, deaths from lightning have been estimated at between 6,000 and 24,000 and injuries at 240,000 a year. In Australia, one to two people have been killed by lightning each year since 2023, according to Kirkby, and more than 100 have been injured. Many experience lasting effects – and not via burn injuries, as commonly thought.

“The burns are usually very minor,” says Prof Mary Ann Cooper, retired from the University of Illinois, Chicago, who has conducted medical studies of lightning victims and released a free book on reducing lightning injury.

The damage is neurological, she says. In the short term it can cause kerauno paralysis (kerauno being Greek for lightning) in the legs or arms. It may cause unconsciousness or confusion akin to concussion. Longer term injuries include learning problems, amnesia, headaches, personality changes, irritability, chronic pain, sleeping problems and dizziness. Many survivors suffer from post-traumatic stress disorder.

“One of my survivors and good friends used to call it black holes that he had in his brain, and he never knew where the little black holes were going to be,” Cooper tells the Guardian.

‘When thunder roars, go indoors’

How can we protect ourselves? First, by understanding the risk.

You don’t have to be in the middle of a storm to be struck, as discovered this month by a man in his 20s who was hit by lightning under a clear blue sky while swimming on the Central Coast of NSW. He was last reported to be in a critical but stable condition.

Use the “flash-to-bang” rule to calculate how far away a pending storm is. “Light travels almost instantly,” Kirkby explains, “but sounds take about three seconds to travel one kilometre.” If you count 30 seconds or less between seeing a flash and hearing the thunder, the storm is up to 10km away and you should head for safety.

The single most important way to protect yourself is to go into a substantial building, say Cooper and Kirkby. “When thunder roars, go indoors.” The next best option is a hard-topped metal vehicle. This isn’t due to the rubber tires but because the current flows over the metal, creating a faraday cage.

After the lightning stops, you should stay sheltered for 30 minutes.

The Australian Bureau of Meteorology warns that there is no safe place outdoors during a storm. But if seeking shelter is not possible, keep your exposure low, Kirkby says. “Keep your feet together and try to find some sort of depressed area so you are not the highest object.”

But don’t seek refuge next to something that is taller than you. If you stand under a tree, for instance, you can be struck by a side flash: if the electrical current goes through the tree it could jump to you. “This happens quite regularly,” Kirkby warns.

Be mindful that lightning deposits up to 1bn volts of electricity at its impact point, which dissipate the further you get from the point of impact.

Kirkby stresses the importance of keeping your feet together – and, whatever you do, don’t lie down. It’s all about equalising the voltage. “Think about a bird sitting on a high-voltage power line with 110,000 to 130,000 volts, and he’s fine, flapping his wings and singing and having a great time,” he says.

But if his wing touches some other object, like a nearby wire, it causes a voltage differential, which causes current to flow. “And it’s the same with people.”

If your feet are apart, it causes a voltage differential that allows ground current to flow through the body, meaning cows can be struck down in whole herds.

Thomas hasn’t noticed any after-effects since the music festival. “Although it would be cool if I had superpowers,” she says.

world.title: Mad about mara: the DIY dance movement helping young Nigerians escape the daily grind
world.snippet: What started as one artist’s response to being cut out of a music video has exploded, becoming a driving force in Nigeria’s cultural land...
world.content:
As a student in the central Nigerian city of Ilorin, Lawal Habeeb Kola loved staying in his hostel room to produce beats rather than returning to his family house in Lagos, the more frenetic city of his birth.

In 2022, one of his beats became popular on TikTok, and a version featuring ad-libbed vocals from a hypeman sent it viral. He was invited to the music video shoot in Lagos and thought his big break had finally come, but when the video was released, he was absent.

“I was in a restaurant and everybody was anticipating seeing me, but my face did not show once,” the 27-year old, known as DJ Khalipha, said. “I felt disgraced. I stopped posting the song.”

Khalipha retreated to his dorm and revisited the DIY “cruise beats” genre of dance music that he had previously worked in. Taking its name from the pidgin expression “catch cruise”, meaning to joke around, cruise beats is a lo-fi, frenetic genre that incorporates amusing voice samples from Nollywood and memes.

Khalipha raised the already fast 115-120 beats per minute of cruise beats to 140-150bpm, added melancholic undertones and named the new style mara, meaning to lose one’s senses. The popularity of the sound soared, eventually crossing over from the Lagos underground and becoming incorporated into the sound of mainstream musicians.

As the genre exploded, Khalipha lost creative control. “It became a trend that every producer and DJ was hopping on,” said Feranmi Abiola, 24, who directed the 2025 documentary Mara Mania. “They were making sounds and whether it was mara sound or not, they would just title it mara fever, mara this, mara that.”

Like its predecessors, mara’s spread was driven by choreography. One dancer, Obi “Odogwu Mara” Madubogwu, named himself after the sound and dropped dance routines on social media weekly, gaining street credibility. His death in unclear circumstances at the age of 26 galvanised interest in mara, especially among young Nigerians for whom posting and responding to dance challenges in his style became a form of escape from poor job prospects in Nigeria’s sluggish economy.

“We’ve seen area boys [street urchins] switching to become dancers,” said the producer Azzi On The Beat, an early adopter of mara who has stayed true to the sound. “The music is spiritual.”

The hectic but harmonious sound has become a fixture at raves, which in Nigeria take the form of street-style block-gatherings populated by young people tired of the markup on alcohol at nightclubs and “bottle culture” – the buying of expensive bottles of champagne and spirts in VIP sections, often as a means of flaunting wealth.

Top musicians have been enlisting the sound in search of new hits, but mara’s originators remain relatively unknown, their work often restricted to the thriving underground “TrenchTok” scene.

Khalipha said bookers assumed that mara DJs would have an air of chaos and violence, due to the raw sound of the music and its association with street culture.

Abiola agreed. “[Mara DJs] are not harmful, but they face stereotypes because of their background, how they look and how they dress,” she said. “In my documentary, I wanted people to see these people for who they were … young people innovating and contributing to the cultural identity of this generation. Regardless of where they are from, they deserve to be taken seriously.”

Without institutional backing, the DJs have been learning how to navigate the music industry on the go. When the samples they were using were flagged for copyright issues, they created their own instrumentals from scratch using plugins.

Many artists are self-funded, investing money earned as social media influencers or from royalties into shooting videos and promotion. Female dancers talk of sexual harassment and financial exploitation in the industry.

“The financial challenges are more apparent for the dancers, because people don’t really take dancers seriously,” said Abiola.

Pointing to a square littered with weeds and rubbish, where goats roamed next to a woman sieving black-eyed peas on a tray, Azzi’s 27-year-old manager, Sangokunle Anuoluwapo – known as Kadima – said: “We do most of our videos here.”

Despite the challenges, the people involved in mara harbour dreams of global traction. Support from the French embassy helped Azzi perform at festivals in Uganda and parts of Europe. A few industry friends on the rise or those who Kadima at one point managed also help intermittently with funding or promoting projects for free.

“I understand what we want for this culture so we keep pushing really hard,” said Kadima. “It’s family work, so we try to split revenues among everybody.”

Azzi was given a leg up from the Footprints of David Art Academy, a children’s dance theatre troupe that held performances behind his mother’s shop. He honed his dancing skills, learned how to drum, and met Kadima there. “We were taught how to fight through tough times,” Azzi said.

The art director Seun Awobajo launched the academy in 2005 with the aim of channelling the energy of disadvantaged children into creative endeavours. “[I had] the notion that no child is useless, they are only used less,” he said.

Awobajo is proud of his former wards and the mara scene more generally. “Being proud is an understatement,” he said. “But I think I feel more fulfilled seeing what they’ve become because these are children who the upper class of the society have written off.”

world.title: ‘I’m no longer a UAE official’: UN hopeful Lana Nusseibeh tries to shake off Sudan record
world.snippet: The US and Russia’s candidate for secretary general is on a charm offensive. Can she overcome London’s resistance to her bid? Lana Nussei...
world.content:
Lana Nusseibeh is in Britain this week, attempting to present herself as a potential future UN secretary general, and shift the focus from her past as a United Arab Emirates diplomat who denied the country’s role in arming a militia accused of war crimes and genocide in Sudan’s four-year civil war.

It is a high-risk strategy that involves meeting ministers, MPs, academics and holding a public event with the UN Association.

Labelled by many British NGOs and others as an apologist for war crimes, Nusseibeh is presenting herself as a skilled diplomat with the network to put the UN back at the centre of mediation, development and human rights.

“These are very geopolitical times,” she said in an interview. “You need a geopolitical secretary general, because the fact is these geopolitical ruptures are not going away. These fissures in the international system are not going to dissolve any time soon.”

Nusseibeh had a setback last Friday, when three permanent members of the UN security council, China, France and the UK, all voted to “discourage” her candidature. The UN’s electoral system requires that she secure nine positive votes from the 15-strong security council, and no discouragement from the permanent five (P5) before being recommended to the UN general assembly.

She has the backing of the US and Russia, and thinks her cause is not lost. “Sometimes, the use of the veto is tactical. Sometimes, it’s a holding position, sometimes it’s a leveraging position. There are a number of different theories”.

The centre of the resistance to Nusseibeh’s candidacy is probably London, and specifically the Foreign Office, the penholder on Sudan at the UN, and this may explain the UK political blitz.

When questioned about her role in Sudan, she asked that her candidacy be seen in the round, highlighting her role in forcing humanitarian aid into Gaza, her support for Afghan women and promoting interfaith tolerance.

“Like every candidate, I come from somewhere, but the independence of the incoming secretary general is the key to their credibility.

“I’ve taken a leave of absence from my role in [the] UAE government in order to independently campaign for this role. But I think that if I was secretary general, Sudan would be the litmus test of success for any incoming secretary because it’s such a horrific humanitarian crisis.”

The war in Sudan, which erupted in April 2023 after a power struggle between the ​military and the Rapid Support Forces, has displaced more than 14 million people and created one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises. Multiple regional powers, including the UAE, have backed different local proxies since the beginning of the conflict in an attempt to win influence and strategic resources.

The UAE has long been accused of supporting the RSF in Sudan, a charge repeatedly denied by Nusseibeh, who has publicly disputed the findings of UN investigators.

A UN panel of experts suggested last month that the UAE had supplied crucial support to the RSF.

Asked if she regretted dissembling during her time as a diplomat, by denying the UAE had armed the RSF, or her personal role in challenging the UN reports critical of the UAE, Nusseibeh said she regretted that “the Sudanese civil war had continued for so long”.

Nusseibeh added: “But I don’t think saying that is enough for the Sudanese people and the people in the surrounding countries where they’ve also felt the impact of this war, or for the victims of sexual violence and in this conflict, the atrocities committed in El Fasher without accountability, and the use of chemical weapons against the civilian population; all of these are a litany of suffering that has been inflicted on the Sudanese people.”

Asked if the UAE had been supplying weapons to the RSF in a breach of a UN embargo, she replied: “I’m aware of the allegations. I haven’t read the last UN panel of experts report, but I’m not going to comment as I’m no longer a UAE official. In this campaign, I am a secretary general candidate.

“As secretary general, I would fully back the findings of all UN panel of experts reports and I’m aware that I think several countries have been mentioned in various reports.”She later added: “I would call out countries that are supplying arms to any of the parties, including those in the RSF … this needs a process that requires accountability for atrocities that have been committed. That it needs to be a process primarily led by the Sudanese people.”

Nusseibeh said she was willing to take risks to mediate and to put UN values, expertise and its development toolkit at the centre of disputes. Her analysis of contemporary diplomacy was that the world had descended into a default setting of non-cooperation, and the UN needed to restate the case for collaboration between nations as being in the self-interest of everyone.

The UN had been missing from too many conflicts, she argued, and she would set up a mediation board to try to use the full UN toolkit, ranging from confidence-building measures to development to secure peace. “What’s missing is this idea of a secretary general that is a strategist and a mediator-in-chief that is looking at the sort of the blips on the dashboard of conflict and saying, ‘How do we deploy to have maximum impact for most effective use of resource and cost?’ Because resources are not going up, they’re going down. I mean, we’re looking at, since 2010, 40% increase in military spending. So we’re using a lot of hard power as countries and systems to deter, but it’s not actually working.”

That would require some prioritisation at the UN – it has 4,000 different open mandates.

Her intelligence and skills as a diplomat are not in question. However, her track record over Sudan is.

One critic said: “It is a very smart strategic play by the UAE that seeks autocratic capture, and then the asset-stripping of the UN and its standards. The UAE would end the UN’s role on climate. It would be a catastrophe.”

The next security council vote is on Monday. By then some of the backmarkers may have dropped out of the race. The diplomats of the P5 may also be clearer on the flexibility of their mandates, in which case the papal conclave may finally produce white smoke.

world.title: At least 31 killed as fuel tanker crash ignites large fire on Cairo highway
world.snippet: Blaze on ring road surrounding Egyptian capital injures at least 21 people and leaves cars and motorcycles charred A crash involving a fu...
world.content:
A crash involving a fuel tanker ignited a huge fire on a highway surrounding Cairo on Wednesday, killing at least 31 people, Egyptian authorities said.

The blaze on the ring road, a key artery that encircles the Egyptian capital, also injured at least 21 people and left more than two dozen cars and motorcycles charred, according to the latest figures released by the health ministry.

State media reported that the fire broke out when the fuel truck overturned. The stretch of the highway where it occurred was in Waraq, a densely populated neighbourhood in Giza, part of the Greater Cairo area, the health ministry said.

At the scene, rescue workers were pulling people out of burning cars. An Associated Press video showed firefighters working to put out the fire spreading among the cars. Hundreds of people gathered near the scene.

Ahmed Sameer, who was stuck in traffic as the road was blocked after the accident, saw the fuel truck and many cars on fire. He said he saw at least eight bodies being removed from burned cars.

“It was a huge fire, the cars got stuck together because of the fire,” he said, describing the fear and panic that followed. “It was a shocking scene.”

The Egyptian president, Abdel Fatah al-Sisi, expressed his condolences to the victims in a statement. The public prosecutor’s office said DNA investigations were under way to identify the victims.

The health minister, Khaled Abdel Ghaffar, said the injured were taken to nearby hospitals and that the death toll was preliminary, raising concerns it could rise further. He later travelled to the scene and to the hospitals, the health ministry said.

The minister’s spokesperson told the state-linked Al-Qahera News that the ring road had been reopened and the remnants of the accident cleared.

Deadly traffic incidents claim thousands of lives every year in Egypt, which has a poor transportation safety record. Speeding, bad roads and poor enforcement of traffic laws are the main reasons behind most of the crashes.

In January 2016, 21 people were killed and 16 were injured in a multicar pileup on a road near the southern province of Beni Suef.

world.title: Swiss tourist killed and British and Americans injured by elephants in Cameroon
world.snippet: Alain Throo, insurance executive based in London, reportedly gored and later died on hike near Mount Cameroon national park A Swiss touri...
world.content:
A Swiss tourist has been killed and British and American tourists have been injured when a group of hikers encountered a herd of elephants in Cameroon.

The group of six tourists, four British, one Swiss and one American, accompanied by local guides, were hiking near the village of Bakingili in the south of the Mount Cameroon national park on 19 November, on a path used by elephants to access a nearby lake, when they encountered the herd of about 15 animals, according to media reports.

The elephants attacked the group and Alain Throo, a Swiss insurance executive based in London, was reportedly gored and one of the guides tossed into a ditch on top of Throo, while the others hid in trees.

Throo had a black eye and was initially responsive and complaining about an injury to his arm, one of the British female hikers told Cameroonian media, which said they had feared he was bleeding internally.

“He said that the elephant attacked him,” an unidentified Cameroonian man added, according to a video posted by CBS Radio Buea FM. “It smashed him.”

Throo later died of his injuries and his body was carried out of the park by a combined team of park staff and the military to a mortuary in the town of Limbeon 21 November. The American hiker was treated at the same hospital and later discharged, according to local media.

One of the British tourists, who said he had hid in a tree stump for two hours, recalled the moment the elephants attacked their group. “I saw these elephants almost next to me. And I thought, if I go down this path as well, I’m going to get hit. So I just moved to the opposite direction. They ran down the path, I ran and hid in a bush. And I heard some screaming.”

Sean McGovern, the UK chief executive of the insurer Axa XL, where Throo had worked for 13 years, confirmed the death, saying Throo was a “valued member of our team, respected colleague and friend whose contribution, professionalism and warmth touched many people”.

Cameroonian media reported that clashes between elephants and local people had been happening for the past 10 years.

Mount Cameroon is the highest mountain in west and central Africa, at more than 4,000 metres. The African forest elephant was declared critically endangered by the International Union for Conservation of Nature in 2021. There are about 195,000 left in the wild, less than 15% of its population 50 years ago, according to the World Wildlife Fund.

Just 5% of forest elephants, which are smaller than their savannah-based counterparts, are found outside central Africa. In Cameroon, there are about 6,000 forest elephants, according to the NGO Global Conservation, which said the species was at risk from poaching syndicates.

A spokesperson for Britain’s Foreign Office said: “We offered assistance after a number of British nationals were injured in Cameroon.”

world.title: Sri Lankan asylum seeker killed himself after being sent by UK to Eswatini
world.snippet: Kishanth Peramalya was denied entry due to sexual assault convictions and sent to Africa where he had no connections The UK sent a Sri La...
world.content:
The UK sent a Sri Lankan asylum seeker who had been convicted of sexual assault to Eswatini, a southern African country to which he had no connection and where he killed himself.

Kishanth Peramalya was part of a group that set sail from India hoping to reach Canada and claim asylum there. The boat was rescued by the Royal Navy in October 2021 when it got into difficulty and brought to Diego Garcia in the remote British Indian Ocean Territory, which hosts a US-UK military base.

In November 2024, the UK allowed 61 migrants to enter from Diego Garcia after a damning UN report about conditions in the camp. However, the then home secretary, Yvette Cooper, denied Peramalya entry to the UK due to his criminal convictions while he was on Diego Garcia for four counts of sexual assault, one count of assault occasioning actual bodily harm and one count of arson. Cooper’s decision was upheld by UK courts.

Peramalya had been granted protection from being returned to Sri Lanka, having been tortured and sexually abused by Sri Lankan military personnel as a teenager. In late March, the Maldives said it would take him for 30 days, according to the BBC. He was then transferred to Eswatini, a country landlocked by South Africa and Mozambique and formerly known as Swaziland, where he killed himself on 13 September.

A draft deal between the UK and Eswatini governments would have committed Downing Street to cover the costs of Peramalya’s resettlement there for three years, according to the BBC, which said the UK was also finalising arrangements for Peramalya to live in Eswatini permanently.

The Guardian has not seen the draft deal. Thabile Mdluli, a spokesperson for Eswatini’s government, said: “The initial arrangement was temporary in nature and intended to safeguard Mr Peramalya’s safety while the government of the United Kingdom worked towards a long-term solution regarding his circumstances.”

She said that no formal agreement was ever reached over Peramalya’s long-term residency status with the UK and declined to comment further on the specific arrangements of his stay in Eswatini or the circumstances around his death.

Mdluli said: “Eswatini has not received any other similar request from the government of the United Kingdom. The government of the Kingdom of Eswatini remains committed to ensuring that any agreements entered into with external partners safeguard national interest as well as the safety and security of Emaswati [Swazi people].”

A UK government spokesperson said: “Keeping the British public safe will always be our first priority, and we will continue to take the decisions necessary to protect the British people. That includes taking steps to ensure high harm foreign criminals cannot enter the UK. We continue to work with the Eswatini authorities in relation to this case.”

Peramalya had post-traumatic stress disorder and attempted suicide multiple times on Diego Garcia, according to a UK high court judgment in February 2025.

Peramalya’s family told the BBC he was initially housed alone in an isolated guesthouse in Eswatini. “My brother did not want to go there at all,” said his sister, speaking from India. “He couldn’t manage being there alone, he was very lonely.”

She said he had called her four times a day and was initially having weekly psychiatric appointments, which were made daily when his mental health deteriorated, as well as having someone brought in to prepare his food.

Peramalya’s relatives said they were not aware of his convictions for sexual offences or any plan to make his transfer to Eswatini permanent.

Eswatini has accepted dozens of third-country deportees from the US since July 2025. In November 2025, its government confirmed it had received $5.1m in exchange for taking up to 160 migrants from the US.
